hero: Explore social work in Ontario: local legislation, professional standards, safeguarding, children and family practice, capacity and reflective learning.

For cross-border work, establish legal responsibility explicitly; the selector does not decide it.

foundations.title: Professional Foundations — Ontario
foundations.action: Confirm registration, professional scope and any additional authority required.
foundations.record: Explain the service, purpose of assessment, informed consent and confidentiality limits. Use supervision to examine bias, cultural safety and the effect of poverty or institutional barriers. Connect continuing competence to changes in practice and the current College programme. A complaint to the College concerns professional conduct or practice. A funding appeal, health-service complaint or privacy complaint has a different route. Clarify which decision the person wants changed and who can address it.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — Ontario
care-support.action: Identify the actual programme and responsible assessment or funding body.
care-support.record: Document daily needs, personal goals, informal support and the effect of service gaps. Separate the eligibility decision, care-plan allocation, any charges and the start of provision. Request reasons and track the relevant complaint, formal review or appeal for the disputed decision. Ontario Health atHome’s feedback process begins with the care coordinator and a patient-services manager and includes formal review for unresolved issues. Certain decisions may be appealed to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board. Check the notice and time limits; a provider-quality complaint is a separate issue.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Ontario
mca.action: Specify the decision and identify which Act and decision-maker apply.
mca.record: Support understanding and assess the relevant understanding-and-appreciation abilities. Check the substitute hierarchy, eligibility and any appointment before seeking a decision. Identify applicable prior capable wishes and use the statutory decision standard where substitute consent is required. The Consent and Capacity Board has review and application functions under the HCCA and other legislation. Rights advice and procedural safeguards depend on the decision and setting. An SDA property assessment should not be substituted for a treating practitioner’s HCCA determination.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Ontario
dols.action: Identify the actual restriction, setting, legal status and the person’s wishes.
dols.record: Separate admission consent from the specific authority for restraint or detention. Check the current setting-specific conditions, documentation, monitoring and any emergency exception. Arrange less restrictive support, rights information and the relevant Board, court or complaints route. The person’s challenge route depends on the measure: a Consent and Capacity Board issue, a mental-health detention review or a long-term-care complaint may address different questions. Obtain advice about disputed confinement and preserve the person’s access to representation.

mha.title: Mental Health — Ontario
mha.action: Identify the exact assessment or admission authority and the evidence supporting its criteria.
mha.record: Record the start, expiry and required next decision for the actual legal status. Arrange the applicable notices, rights advice and access to legal representation or Board review. Assess treatment consent separately and coordinate a real discharge and follow-up plan. The Consent and Capacity Board reviews relevant involuntary-status and capacity matters. Rights advice is important when statutory notices or findings trigger it. A voluntary patient’s wish to leave requires the appropriate legal response; staff should not describe the person as detained without identifying a lawful basis.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — Ontario
safeguarding.action: Identify the adult’s setting and the specific suspected abuse, neglect, unlawful conduct or financial misuse.
safeguarding.record: Apply the reporting threshold and recipient under the relevant Act, including any applicable exception. Arrange immediate safety and safe contact while considering consent, coercion and information sharing. Confirm receipt, responsibility and ongoing practical support rather than treating the report as the end of the response. Explain the relevant Ministry, RHRA, police or service complaint route. A reporting obligation does not itself authorise a worker to take over the adult’s finances or accommodation. Capacity and representative-authority questions require their own framework.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Ontario
children.action: Identify the child’s age, concern and reasonable grounds under the CYFSA.
children.record: Make the required direct report to the appropriate society and further reports when new grounds arise. Record the child’s words and immediate safety needs without conducting an unnecessary parallel investigation. Coordinate family support and participation, identifying any applicable Indigenous service authority and legal framework. Explain the society’s role, support and applicable court or review processes. Confidentiality has statutory limits where reporting is required. A report about an older teenager should not be dismissed simply because the same mandatory provision does not apply.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Ontario
rights.action: Identify the service decision, relevant protected ground and accommodation required.
rights.record: Check whether PHIPA or another privacy regime governs the organisation and proposed disclosure. Separate consent to service, consent to treatment and consent or other authority for information sharing. Record evidence and disagreement and explain access, correction, privacy complaints and the relevant rights remedy. The Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario addresses privacy matters within its jurisdiction; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses applicable Code claims. A College complaint has a different purpose. Help the person seek the remedy relevant to the disputed act and obtain timely advice.

sources.title: Ontario Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: The Ontario College of Social Workers and Social Service Workers (OCSWSSW) regulates two professions with distinct scopes. Its Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice address relationships, competence, responsibilities, records, confidentiality, fees, communication and boundaries. Use the current standards alongside the legislation applying to the task.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Registration does not make every registrant a designated capacity assessor or confer every controlled-act or statutory power. Establish the role, competence and additional requirements before undertaking specialist work. Identify whether the employer is a health-information custodian, a public body or another organisation because that affects records and disclosure duties.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Confirm registration, professional scope and any additional authority required. Explain the service, purpose of assessment, informed consent and confidentiality limits. Use supervision to examine bias, cultural safety and the effect of poverty or institutional barriers. Connect continuing competence to changes in practice and the current College programme.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: A complaint to the College concerns professional conduct or practice. A funding appeal, health-service complaint or privacy complaint has a different route. Clarify which decision the person wants changed and who can address it.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating College registration as proof of every specialist assessment qualification.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: Ontario Health atHome coordinates important home-care and long-term-care placement functions. Distinguish home-care eligibility, the amount or type of service, placement eligibility and a provider’s delivery. Income support, developmental services, housing and privately arranged care have separate rules.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Ontario Health atHome identifies appealable matters including eligibility, service amounts, exclusion or discontinuation of services and long-term-care admission eligibility. Discussion with a coordinator, management review and an external appeal are not the same step. Obtain the decision and the appropriate route in writing.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the actual programme and responsible assessment or funding body. Document daily needs, personal goals, informal support and the effect of service gaps. Separate the eligibility decision, care-plan allocation, any charges and the start of provision. Request reasons and track the relevant complaint, formal review or appeal for the disputed decision.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Ontario Health atHome’s feedback process begins with the care coordinator and a patient-services manager and includes formal review for unresolved issues. Certain decisions may be appealed to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board. Check the notice and time limits; a provider-quality complaint is a separate issue.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing a complaint about a worker with an appeal against the amount of funded care.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: The Health Care Consent Act 1996 (HCCA) distinguishes treatment, admission to a care facility and personal-assistance decisions. Its capacity test asks whether the person understands relevant information and appreciates reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding or not deciding. The Substitute Decisions Act 1992 separately addresses property and personal-care arrangements.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: For HCCA substitute consent, apply the statutory hierarchy and eligibility requirements. Applicable prior capable wishes matter; where no applicable wish governs, the statutory best-interests framework applies. A power of attorney must be checked for scope and operation rather than assumed to cover every decision.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Specify the decision and identify which Act and decision-maker apply. Support understanding and assess the relevant understanding-and-appreciation abilities. Check the substitute hierarchy, eligibility and any appointment before seeking a decision. Identify applicable prior capable wishes and use the statutory decision standard where substitute consent is required.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Consent and Capacity Board has review and application functions under the HCCA and other legislation. Rights advice and procedural safeguards depend on the decision and setting. An SDA property assessment should not be substituted for a treating practitioner’s HCCA determination.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Equating financial incapacity with treatment incapacity or ignoring applicable prior capable wishes.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: Admission to a care facility, consent to treatment and authority to restrain or confine are distinct questions. The HCCA, Mental Health Act and setting-specific legislation such as the Fixing Long-Term Care Act 2021 may be relevant. Read the provision and its commencement note: an enacted future amendment is not an operative confinement power.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Long-term-care restraint requirements and mental-health detention procedures should not be treated as one system. A substitute’s agreement to admission does not by itself explain every locked-door arrangement or restraint used after admission.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the actual restriction, setting, legal status and the person’s wishes. Separate admission consent from the specific authority for restraint or detention. Check the current setting-specific conditions, documentation, monitoring and any emergency exception. Arrange less restrictive support, rights information and the relevant Board, court or complaints route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The person’s challenge route depends on the measure: a Consent and Capacity Board issue, a mental-health detention review or a long-term-care complaint may address different questions. Obtain advice about disputed confinement and preserve the person’s access to representation.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating consent to placement as blanket consent to confinement or relying on an uncommenced amendment.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: Ontario’s Mental Health Act provides assessment and involuntary-admission routes. A Form 1 permits a psychiatric assessment period of up to 72 hours when its criteria are met; it is not itself indefinite detention or automatic authority for every treatment. Subsequent involuntary status requires the applicable certification and safeguards.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Act has different routes and criteria, including provisions relating to harm or serious impairment and specific deterioration circumstances. Apply the full relevant provision rather than reducing every route to a single danger test. Treatment consent remains a separate HCCA question.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the exact assessment or admission authority and the evidence supporting its criteria. Record the start, expiry and required next decision for the actual legal status. Arrange the applicable notices, rights advice and access to legal representation or Board review. Assess treatment consent separately and coordinate a real discharge and follow-up plan.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Consent and Capacity Board reviews relevant involuntary-status and capacity matters. Rights advice is important when statutory notices or findings trigger it. A voluntary patient’s wish to leave requires the appropriate legal response; staff should not describe the person as detained without identifying a lawful basis.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Confusing an assessment hold, involuntary admission and authority to treat.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: Ontario has setting-specific adult-protection and reporting rules. The Fixing Long-Term Care Act 2021 and Retirement Homes Act 2010 contain reporting obligations for specified suspected harms, with different recipients and statutory exceptions. Community elder-abuse concerns require a different analysis; do not assume a single universal adult-reporting duty.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: For long-term-care matters, identify the Ministry’s reporting route; retirement-home matters involve the Retirement Homes Regulatory Authority (RHRA). Police, healthcare, the Public Guardian and Trustee or other supports may also be relevant depending on the facts and authority involved.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the adult’s setting and the specific suspected abuse, neglect, unlawful conduct or financial misuse. Apply the reporting threshold and recipient under the relevant Act, including any applicable exception. Arrange immediate safety and safe contact while considering consent, coercion and information sharing. Confirm receipt, responsibility and ongoing practical support rather than treating the report as the end of the response.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the relevant Ministry, RHRA, police or service complaint route. A reporting obligation does not itself authorise a worker to take over the adult’s finances or accommodation. Capacity and representative-authority questions require their own framework.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using one adult-safeguarding process for community, retirement-home and long-term-care settings.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: The Child, Youth and Family Services Act 2017 (CYFSA) includes a direct and ongoing duty to report specified protection concerns to a children’s aid society where there are reasonable grounds to suspect them. A person with the duty must report directly rather than rely on a manager or colleague.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The mandatory duty in this provision does not apply in the same way to 16- and 17-year-olds, although concerns about them may be reported and services may be available. Age and the actual statutory ground matter. Indigenous child and family service jurisdiction and applicable community laws also need checking where relevant.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the child’s age, concern and reasonable grounds under the CYFSA. Make the required direct report to the appropriate society and further reports when new grounds arise. Record the child’s words and immediate safety needs without conducting an unnecessary parallel investigation. Coordinate family support and participation, identifying any applicable Indigenous service authority and legal framework.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain the society’s role, support and applicable court or review processes. Confidentiality has statutory limits where reporting is required. A report about an older teenager should not be dismissed simply because the same mandatory provision does not apply.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Delegating the report to a manager or applying the under-16 mandatory rule without checking the young person’s age.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in Ontario practice guide?
cards.answer: The Ontario Human Rights Code protects against discrimination in covered areas and requires accommodation within the applicable legal framework. The Canadian Charter has its own scope concerning government action. Do not assume the same rights mechanism applies to every private and public service.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Personal Health Information Protection Act 2004 (PHIPA) applies according to the role of the custodian, agent and information. Other organisations may be governed by different privacy laws. College confidentiality and recording standards operate alongside those laws, not in place of them.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the service decision, relevant protected ground and accommodation required. Check whether PHIPA or another privacy regime governs the organisation and proposed disclosure. Separate consent to service, consent to treatment and consent or other authority for information sharing. Record evidence and disagreement and explain access, correction, privacy complaints and the relevant rights remedy.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario addresses privacy matters within its jurisdiction; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses applicable Code claims. A College complaint has a different purpose. Help the person seek the remedy relevant to the disputed act and obtain timely advice.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming every social worker is operating under the same health-information consent rules.

glossaryTerms.term: Ontario College of Social Workers and Social Service Workers (OCSWSSW)
glossaryTerms.definition: The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A manager asks a registered social worker to complete a statutory assessment requiring a particular assessor designation.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the legal requirements and the worker’s actual designation, competence and scope. Arrange an appropriately authorised assessor if needed. Continue gathering relevant social evidence without representing that work as the statutory determination.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: An adult’s home-care visits are reduced although their mobility has worsened. The family is told only to complain to the visiting agency.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Establish who reduced the allocation and obtain the reassessment and reasons. Address immediate safety with the coordinator and use the relevant service-decision review or appeal. Pursue a provider complaint separately if the agency also failed to deliver the authorised visits.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A hospital patient understands a proposed treatment but has a property guardian. Staff ask the guardian to consent without assessing treatment capacity.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the patient’s ability for the treatment decision and provide support. Read the guardian’s powers and identify the correct HCCA route only if substitute consent is needed. Financial guardianship is not evidence that the patient cannot consent to treatment.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A long-term-care home says a daughter’s admission consent also permits a standing order preventing her father from leaving.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Read the admission and representative documents, assess the father’s wishes and the actual restriction, and identify the separate legal basis relied on. Check the current restraint and confinement provisions rather than assuming that admission consent answers the liberty question.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A patient is held on Form 1 and a team assumes that this both permits medication without consent and authorises a longer stay.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the assessment period and whether a further lawful admission status is required. Apply HCCA consent separately to the proposed medication. Explain rights and arrange the relevant advice; neither the assessment form nor clinical preference resolves all three decisions.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker hears about financial misuse affecting a retirement-home resident and is told to report only to the home’s manager.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the statutory reporting duty and RHRA route; internal reporting may not satisfy it. Address immediate access to funds and support, record the adult’s account and consider any separate police or representative concern.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker raises a new concern about a 12-year-old and a manager says an earlier report by another worker covers it.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the new reasonable grounds and make the required direct report. Record what is new, the child’s account and immediate safety arrangements. An earlier report does not remove the ongoing personal duty.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — Ontario
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A social worker in a community organisation assumes they can share a complete file using a hospital’s implied-consent practice.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Identify the organisation’s legal status, purpose of disclosure and applicable law. Do not import the hospital’s framework without checking. Obtain or establish the proper basis, limit the disclosure and explain the person’s choices and complaint route.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Ontario College of Social Workers and Social Service Workers (OCSWSSW) regulates two professions with distinct scopes. Its Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice address relationships, competence, responsibilities, records, confidentiality, fees, communication and boundaries. Use the current standards alongside the legislation applying to the task.

Registration does not make every registrant a designated capacity assessor or confer every controlled-act or statutory power. Establish the role, competence and additional requirements before undertaking specialist work. Identify whether the employer is a health-information custodian, a public body or another organisation because that affects records and disclosure duties.

Local pathway:
Confirm registration, professional scope and any additional authority required.
Explain the service, purpose of assessment, informed consent and confidentiality limits.
Use supervision to examine bias, cultural safety and the effect of poverty or institutional barriers.
Connect continuing competence to changes in practice and the current College programme.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
A complaint to the College concerns professional conduct or practice. A funding appeal, health-service complaint or privacy complaint has a different route. Clarify which decision the person wants changed and who can address it.

Sources:
https://www.ocswssw.org/sop/
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/98s31

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Ontario Health atHome coordinates important home-care and long-term-care placement functions. Distinguish home-care eligibility, the amount or type of service, placement eligibility and a provider’s delivery. Income support, developmental services, housing and privately arranged care have separate rules.

Ontario Health atHome identifies appealable matters including eligibility, service amounts, exclusion or discontinuation of services and long-term-care admission eligibility. Discussion with a coordinator, management review and an external appeal are not the same step. Obtain the decision and the appropriate route in writing.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual programme and responsible assessment or funding body.
Document daily needs, personal goals, informal support and the effect of service gaps.
Separate the eligibility decision, care-plan allocation, any charges and the start of provision.
Request reasons and track the relevant complaint, formal review or appeal for the disputed decision.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Ontario Health atHome’s feedback process begins with the care coordinator and a patient-services manager and includes formal review for unresolved issues. Certain decisions may be appealed to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board. Check the notice and time limits; a provider-quality complaint is a separate issue.

Sources:
https://www.ontariohealthathome.ca/contact/patient-experience-and-feedback/
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/19c05c

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Health Care Consent Act 1996 (HCCA) distinguishes treatment, admission to a care facility and personal-assistance decisions. Its capacity test asks whether the person understands relevant information and appreciates reasonably foreseeable consequences of deciding or not deciding. The Substitute Decisions Act 1992 separately addresses property and personal-care arrangements.

For HCCA substitute consent, apply the statutory hierarchy and eligibility requirements. Applicable prior capable wishes matter; where no applicable wish governs, the statutory best-interests framework applies. A power of attorney must be checked for scope and operation rather than assumed to cover every decision.

Local pathway:
Specify the decision and identify which Act and decision-maker apply.
Support understanding and assess the relevant understanding-and-appreciation abilities.
Check the substitute hierarchy, eligibility and any appointment before seeking a decision.
Identify applicable prior capable wishes and use the statutory decision standard where substitute consent is required.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Consent and Capacity Board has review and application functions under the HCCA and other legislation. Rights advice and procedural safeguards depend on the decision and setting. An SDA property assessment should not be substituted for a treating practitioner’s HCCA determination.

Sources:
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96h02
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/92s30

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Admission to a care facility, consent to treatment and authority to restrain or confine are distinct questions. The HCCA, Mental Health Act and setting-specific legislation such as the Fixing Long-Term Care Act 2021 may be relevant. Read the provision and its commencement note: an enacted future amendment is not an operative confinement power.

Long-term-care restraint requirements and mental-health detention procedures should not be treated as one system. A substitute’s agreement to admission does not by itself explain every locked-door arrangement or restraint used after admission.

Local pathway:
Identify the actual restriction, setting, legal status and the person’s wishes.
Separate admission consent from the specific authority for restraint or detention.
Check the current setting-specific conditions, documentation, monitoring and any emergency exception.
Arrange less restrictive support, rights information and the relevant Board, court or complaints route.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The person’s challenge route depends on the measure: a Consent and Capacity Board issue, a mental-health detention review or a long-term-care complaint may address different questions. Obtain advice about disputed confinement and preserve the person’s access to representation.

Sources:
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96h02
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/21f39
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90m07

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Ontario’s Mental Health Act provides assessment and involuntary-admission routes. A Form 1 permits a psychiatric assessment period of up to 72 hours when its criteria are met; it is not itself indefinite detention or automatic authority for every treatment. Subsequent involuntary status requires the applicable certification and safeguards.

The Act has different routes and criteria, including provisions relating to harm or serious impairment and specific deterioration circumstances. Apply the full relevant provision rather than reducing every route to a single danger test. Treatment consent remains a separate HCCA question.

Local pathway:
Identify the exact assessment or admission authority and the evidence supporting its criteria.
Record the start, expiry and required next decision for the actual legal status.
Arrange the applicable notices, rights advice and access to legal representation or Board review.
Assess treatment consent separately and coordinate a real discharge and follow-up plan.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Consent and Capacity Board reviews relevant involuntary-status and capacity matters. Rights advice is important when statutory notices or findings trigger it. A voluntary patient’s wish to leave requires the appropriate legal response; staff should not describe the person as detained without identifying a lawful basis.

Sources:
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90m07
https://www.ontario.ca/files/2024-05/moh-information-guide-voluntary-patients-en-2024-05-21.pdf
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96h02

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Ontario has setting-specific adult-protection and reporting rules. The Fixing Long-Term Care Act 2021 and Retirement Homes Act 2010 contain reporting obligations for specified suspected harms, with different recipients and statutory exceptions. Community elder-abuse concerns require a different analysis; do not assume a single universal adult-reporting duty.

For long-term-care matters, identify the Ministry’s reporting route; retirement-home matters involve the Retirement Homes Regulatory Authority (RHRA). Police, healthcare, the Public Guardian and Trustee or other supports may also be relevant depending on the facts and authority involved.

Local pathway:
Identify the adult’s setting and the specific suspected abuse, neglect, unlawful conduct or financial misuse.
Apply the reporting threshold and recipient under the relevant Act, including any applicable exception.
Arrange immediate safety and safe contact while considering consent, coercion and information sharing.
Confirm receipt, responsibility and ongoing practical support rather than treating the report as the end of the response.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the relevant Ministry, RHRA, police or service complaint route. A reporting obligation does not itself authorise a worker to take over the adult’s finances or accommodation. Capacity and representative-authority questions require their own framework.

Sources:
https://www.ontario.ca/page/information-about-elder-abuse
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/10r11
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/21f39

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Child, Youth and Family Services Act 2017 (CYFSA) includes a direct and ongoing duty to report specified protection concerns to a children’s aid society where there are reasonable grounds to suspect them. A person with the duty must report directly rather than rely on a manager or colleague.

The mandatory duty in this provision does not apply in the same way to 16- and 17-year-olds, although concerns about them may be reported and services may be available. Age and the actual statutory ground matter. Indigenous child and family service jurisdiction and applicable community laws also need checking where relevant.

Local pathway:
Identify the child’s age, concern and reasonable grounds under the CYFSA.
Make the required direct report to the appropriate society and further reports when new grounds arise.
Record the child’s words and immediate safety needs without conducting an unnecessary parallel investigation.
Coordinate family support and participation, identifying any applicable Indigenous service authority and legal framework.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain the society’s role, support and applicable court or review processes. Confidentiality has statutory limits where reporting is required. A report about an older teenager should not be dismissed simply because the same mandatory provision does not apply.

Sources:
https://files.ontario.ca/pdf-3/mccss-report-child-abuse-and-neglect-en-2022-03-31.pdf
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/17c14

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
Ontario practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Ontario Human Rights Code protects against discrimination in covered areas and requires accommodation within the applicable legal framework. The Canadian Charter has its own scope concerning government action. Do not assume the same rights mechanism applies to every private and public service.

The Personal Health Information Protection Act 2004 (PHIPA) applies according to the role of the custodian, agent and information. Other organisations may be governed by different privacy laws. College confidentiality and recording standards operate alongside those laws, not in place of them.

Local pathway:
Identify the service decision, relevant protected ground and accommodation required.
Check whether PHIPA or another privacy regime governs the organisation and proposed disclosure.
Separate consent to service, consent to treatment and consent or other authority for information sharing.
Record evidence and disagreement and explain access, correction, privacy complaints and the relevant rights remedy.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario addresses privacy matters within its jurisdiction; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses applicable Code claims. A College complaint has a different purpose. Help the person seek the remedy relevant to the disputed act and obtain timely advice.

Sources:
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/04p03
https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19
https://www.ocswssw.org/2018/10/03/practice-notes-whats-legislation-got-to-do-with-it/
